segments.narration: Doctors told the King a woman was birthing rabbits. Godalming, Surrey, autumn 1726. Mary Toft, a clothier's wife, twenty-five years old.
A Guildford surgeon delivered nine of the creatures. London's medical elite came down to watch, and George the First sent his own surgeons.
One of them, Cyriacus Ahlers, examined a rabbit and found corn, hay and straw in its gut. A newborn had been eating hay?
On the fourth of December a nobleman found out Toft's husband had been buying young rabbits. She confessed three days later.
She had hoped for fame and a royal pension. Surgeon John Howard was fined eight hundred pounds, and Hogarth put the whole circus into a print.

verdicts.claim: In late 1726 Mary Toft, a clothier's wife from Godalming in Surrey, claimed to be giving birth to rabbits, and the case reached King George I's court.
verdicts.note: 75% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Guildford surgeon John Howard delivered the specimens, a report of 19 November 1726 counted nine creatures, and the King sent his own surgeons including Cyriacus Ahlers.
verdicts.note: 89% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Ahlers arrived on 20 November 1726, suspected a hoax, and found dung in one rabbit containing corn, hay and straw, which pointed away from a birth.
verdicts.note: 69% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: On 4 December 1726 Thomas Onslow discovered that Toft's husband had been buying young rabbits, and Toft confessed on 7 December 1726.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: on 4 December Thomas Onslow, 2nd Baron Onslow, discovered Joshua Toft buying young rabbits, and a porter confessed to a bribe the same day; Toft confessed on 7 December before Manningham and Douglas.

verdicts.claim: Toft's stated motives included fame and the hope of a royal pension; surgeon John Howard was fined 800 pounds on 7 January 1727 and Hogarth satirised the affair in a 1726 print.
verdicts.note: Hoaxes.org gives the motives as a desire for fame and hope of a royal pension; Wikipedia gives Howard's 800-pound fine on 7 January 1727 and Hogarth's Cunicularii (1726).
